biomarkers.high_causes: Dietary acid load, reduced kidney clearance, ketosis, dehydration

biomarkers.name: Urea
biomarkers.description: Urea is a waste product of protein metabolism, filtered by the kidneys. It can reflect both kidney function and protein intake. Marina's urea of 4.4 is within the optimal range, suggesting adequate kidney clearance and a moderate level of protein intake.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein diet, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, dehydration, high protein diet, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Creatinine
biomarkers.description: Creatinine is a waste product of muscle metabolism, filtered by the kidneys at a relatively constant rate. It is the standard marker used to estimate kidney filtration. Marina's creatinine of 58 is within the optimal range, consistent with her small frame and low muscle mass.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low muscle mass, malnutrition, pregnancy
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, dehydration, high muscle mass, intense exercise, high meat diet

biomarkers.name: Estimated GFR
biomarkers.description: The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is calculated from creatinine and represents how well the kidneys filter waste from the blood. Marina's eGFR is reported as greater than 90, which is the normal threshold. Her Cystatin C-based eGFR of 107 provides a more accurate measurement and confirms excellent kidney function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, acute kidney injury, dehydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperfiltration (early diabetes), pregnancy, high cardiac output

biomarkers.name: Cystatin-C
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C is a protein produced by all nucleated cells at a constant rate, filtered by the kidneys. Unlike creatinine, it is not affected by muscle mass, making it a more reliable marker of kidney function in people with low or high muscle mass. Marina's Cystatin C of 0.86 is within the optimal range, giving a calculated eGFR of 107, which confirms excellent kidney function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hyperthyroidism, corticosteroid use
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, hypothyroidism, inflammation

biomarkers.name: Cystatin C eGFR
biomarkers.description: This eGFR is calculated using Cystatin C rather than creatinine. At 107, it confirms that Marina's kidneys are filtering at an excellent rate for her age, with no sign of any impairment.
biomarkers.low_causes: Kidney disease, ageing
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperfiltration

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C) is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: Urea:Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: Urea:Creatinine Ratio is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein intake, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high protein intake, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haemoglobin is the iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue in the body. Marina's haemoglobin of 121 is just barely within the normal range, sitting one point above the lower limit of 120. At this level she is at the boundary of clinical anaemia. Given her severely depleted iron stores (ferritin 5, transferrin saturation 7.1%), her haemoglobin is likely to fall further without intervention, which would explain her ongoing fatigue and low energy.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12 or folate deficiency, chronic disease, blood loss, bone marrow disorders
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia, smoking

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Count
biomarkers.description: The red blood cell count measures the number of red cells per litre of blood. Marina's RBC of 4.67 is within the optimal range. Interestingly, despite her severe iron deficiency, her bone marrow is maintaining a high number of red cells, but each cell is smaller (low MCV) and carries less haemoglobin (low MCH) than it should. This is the classic pattern of iron deficiency: the body tries to maintain the number of cells but cannot fill them properly.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, chronic disease, blood loss
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia, smoking

biomarkers.name: Haematocrit
biomarkers.description: Haematocrit measures the proportion of blood volume that is occupied by red blood cells. Marina's haematocrit of 0.358 is marginally below the lower limit of 0.36. This is consistent with her iron deficiency: although she has a good number of red cells, each one is smaller than normal, so they collectively take up slightly less of the blood volume than they should.
biomarkers.low_causes: Anaemia, iron deficiency, blood loss, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia

biomarkers.name: MCV
biomarkers.description: MCV (mean corpuscular volume) measures the average size of each red blood cell. Marina's MCV of 76.6 is below the lower limit of 83, confirming microcytic (small) red cells. This is the hallmark of iron deficiency: without enough iron to build haemoglobin, the bone marrow produces smaller cells. This finding, together with low MCH and high RDW, forms a classic iron deficiency picture.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, chronic disease, lead poisoning
biomarkers.high_causes: B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, liver disease, medications

biomarkers.name: MCH
biomarkers.description: MCH (mean corpuscular haemoglobin) measures the average amount of haemoglobin in each red blood cell. Marina's MCH of 25.9 is below the lower limit of 27, meaning each red cell is carrying less oxygen-transporting haemoglobin than it should. This is directly caused by insufficient iron to build haemoglobin molecules, and is another component of the iron deficiency anaemia picture.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: MCHC
biomarkers.description: MCHC (mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration) measures the average concentration of haemoglobin within each red cell. Marina's MCHC of 338 is within the normal and optimal range, meaning that although each cell is smaller and carries less total haemoglobin, the concentration of haemoglobin within each cell is maintained. This is typical of early to moderate iron deficiency before MCHC itself begins to fall.
biomarkers.low_causes: Severe iron deficiency, thalassaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: Hereditary spherocytosis, sample artefact

biomarkers.name: RDW
biomarkers.description: RDW (red cell distribution width) measures the variation in size among red blood cells. A high RDW means there is a wide spread between the smallest and largest cells. Marina's RDW of 17.7% is significantly above the upper limit of 14%, indicating a mixed population of older normal-sized red cells and newer smaller iron-starved cells. This is a sensitive early marker of iron deficiency and confirms that the iron depletion has been developing over time.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, B12 or folate deficiency, mixed nutritional deficiency, thalassaemia, chronic disease

biomarkers.name: Platelets
biomarkers.description: Platelets are the blood cells responsible for clotting. Marina's platelet count of 285 is within the optimal range, indicating normal clotting capacity. Iron deficiency can sometimes cause reactive thrombocytosis (elevated platelets), but her count remains within a healthy range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Viral infections, bone marrow disorders, medications, liver disease, autoimmune
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency (reactive), infection, inflammation, post-splenectomy

biomarkers.name: MPV
biomarkers.description: MPV (mean platelet volume) measures the average size of platelets. Larger platelets tend to be younger and more reactive. Marina's MPV of 9.4 is within the optimal range, indicating normal platelet production by the bone marrow.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic inflammation, bone marrow suppression
biomarkers.high_causes: Platelet destruction, immune thrombocytopenia, hyperthyroidism

biomarkers.name: White Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The total white blood cell count reflects the overall activity of the immune system. Marina's WBC of 4.33 is within the laboratory range but near the lower end and below the optimal floor of 4.5. This is being driven by her low neutrophil count rather than any deficiency across all white cell types. Her lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils are all within range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Benign ethnic neutropenia, viral infection, medications, autoimmune disease, bone marrow suppression
biomarkers.high_causes: Infection, inflammation, stress, corticosteroids, smoking, leukaemia

biomarkers.name: Neutrophils
biomarkers.description: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and form the first line of defence against bacterial and fungal infections. Marina's neutrophils at 1.74 are below the lower limit of 2.0. Mild neutropenia (low neutrophil count) in an otherwise well person of Eastern European ancestry is most commonly due to benign ethnic neutropenia, a harmless normal variant that is well documented in people from this background. It does not increase infection risk and does not require treatment, but it is worth her GP being aware of as a baseline value for future reference.
biomarkers.low_causes: Benign ethnic neutropenia, viral infection, autoimmune disease, medications, B12/folate deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Bacterial infection, inflammation, stress, smoking, corticosteroids

biomarkers.name: Lymphocytes
biomarkers.description: Lymphocytes are the white blood cells responsible for adaptive immunity, including T-cells that fight viruses and B-cells that produce antibodies. Marina's lymphocytes at 2.19 are within the optimal range, indicating a healthy adaptive immune system.
biomarkers.low_causes: HIV, immunosuppressive drugs, severe infection, corticosteroids
biomarkers.high_causes: Viral infection, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: Monocytes
biomarkers.description: Monocytes are white blood cells that develop into macrophages in tissues, where they engulf pathogens and cellular debris. Marina's monocytes at 0.33 are within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Bone marrow suppression, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, chronic inflammation

biomarkers.name: Eosinophils
biomarkers.description: Eosinophils are white blood cells involved in fighting parasites and mediating allergic responses. Marina's eosinophils at 0.05 are within the optimal range, with no sign of allergic activity or parasitic infection.
biomarkers.low_causes: Corticosteroid use, acute stress
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergies, asthma, parasitic infection, drug reactions, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: Basophils
biomarkers.description: Basophils are the least common white blood cells, involved in allergic reactions and inflammation. Marina's basophils at 0.02 are at the lower boundary of the normal range, which is a normal finding as basophils are always present in very small numbers.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding, corticosteroid use, hyperthyroidism
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergic reactions, chronic inflammation, hypothyroidism, myeloproliferative disorders

biomarkers.name: Reticulocyte Count (%)
biomarkers.description: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells freshly released from the bone marrow. The percentage reflects how actively the marrow is producing new red cells. Marina's reticulocyte percentage of 0.79% is within the laboratory range but below the optimal floor of 0.8%. In the context of her iron deficiency, the marrow does not have sufficient iron to ramp up production as it normally would in response to anaemia.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, chronic kidney disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Active bleeding, haemolysis, response to iron/B12 treatment, bone marrow recovery

biomarkers.name: Reticulocytes Absolute
biomarkers.description: The absolute reticulocyte count gives the actual number of young red cells being released into the blood per litre. Marina's absolute reticulocyte count of 36.9 is below the lower limit of 50, confirming that her bone marrow output is suppressed. This is an inappropriately low reticulocyte response for someone whose haemoglobin is at the lower boundary of normal, meaning the marrow should be producing more new cells but cannot because it lacks the iron to do so.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, aplastic anaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemolysis, acute blood loss, response to treatment, bone marrow recovery

biomarkers.name: Ferritin
biomarkers.description: Ferritin is the body's storage form of iron. It reflects how much iron is held in reserve in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Marina's ferritin of 5 is critically low, well below the laboratory lower limit of 10 and far below the optimal floor of 40. At this level, iron stores are essentially depleted. This is the central finding driving her microcytic red cell changes (low MCV, low MCH, high RDW), her suppressed reticulocyte production, and almost certainly contributing significantly to her fatigue and hair thinning.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency from blood loss (menstrual, gastrointestinal), inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption, pregnancy
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron overload, haemochromatosis, inflammation (acute phase reactant), liver disease, infection

biomarkers.name: Serum Iron
biomarkers.description: Serum iron measures the amount of iron circulating in the blood, bound to the transport protein transferrin. Marina's serum iron of 6.1 is well below the lower limit of 9, confirming that there is insufficient iron in circulation to support normal red blood cell production. Serum iron can fluctuate during the day and with meals, but at this level the finding is unequivocal.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, chronic disease, malabsorption, blood loss
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemochromatosis, iron supplementation, haemolysis, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Transferrin
biomarkers.description: Transferrin is the main iron transport protein in the blood. The liver produces more transferrin when iron stores are low, essentially building more 'trucks' to search for and carry any available iron. Marina's transferrin of 3.42 is within the upper portion of the range, which is a physiologically appropriate response to her depleted iron stores.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron overload, chronic inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, oestrogen use

biomarkers.name: Transferrin Saturation
biomarkers.description: Transferrin saturation measures what percentage of the available transferrin molecules are actually carrying iron. Marina's transferrin saturation of just 7.1% is far below the lower limit of 18%, meaning the vast majority of her iron transport protein is circulating empty, unable to find iron to carry. This is one of the most definitive markers of true iron deficiency and confirms that the supply of iron to the bone marrow is severely compromised.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, chronic disease, malabsorption
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemochromatosis, iron supplementation, haemolysis, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity
biomarkers.description: TIBC (total iron binding capacity) measures the maximum amount of iron that the blood could carry if every transferrin molecule were fully loaded. When iron stores are depleted, the body increases transferrin production, which raises TIBC. Marina's TIBC of 77.4 is above the upper limit of 76.1, confirming the body's compensatory attempt to scavenge more iron from the limited supply available.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron overload, chronic inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, pregnancy

biomarkers.name: TSH
biomarkers.description: TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland to tell the thyroid how much hormone to produce. When thyroid hormone levels are insufficient, the pituitary releases more TSH to try to stimulate the thyroid. Marina's TSH of 6.41 is above the upper limit of 4.78, indicating that despite taking levothyroxine, her thyroid hormone replacement is not fully optimised. Her pituitary gland is still having to push harder than it should to maintain adequate thyroid hormone levels.
biomarkers.low_causes: Excess thyroid medication, hyperthyroidism, pituitary disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Hypothyroidism, insufficient replacement dose, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, iodine deficiency

biomarkers.name: Free T4
biomarkers.description: Free T4 (thyroxine) is the main hormone produced by the thyroid gland and replaced by levothyroxine medication. It is the circulating reservoir that gets converted to the active form, T3. Marina's FT4 of 19.9 is within the optimal range of 14 to 20, which is reassuring and shows that her levothyroxine is providing adequate T4 levels. The issue is that the pituitary (TSH 6.41) is having to work harder than it should to maintain this level, suggesting that a modest dose increase would bring TSH into the optimal range without pushing FT4 too high.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypothyroidism, insufficient levothyroxine dose, pituitary disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Excess thyroid medication, hyperthyroidism, early pregnancy

biomarkers.name: Free T3
biomarkers.description: Free T3 (triiodothyronine) is the most active thyroid hormone. It is produced by conversion from T4 in tissues throughout the body and drives metabolic rate, energy production, and cellular function. Marina's FT3 of 4.5 sits at the lower boundary of the optimal range of 4.5 to 6.5. She is converting T4 to T3 adequately but at the lower end of ideal. Optimising her TSH with a dose increase may improve T3 production.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypothyroidism, illness (sick euthyroid), selenium deficiency, caloric restriction
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism, excess thyroid medication, T3 supplementation

biomarkers.name: TPO Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies are autoantibodies that target an enzyme in the thyroid gland essential for thyroid hormone production. Their presence confirms an autoimmune process attacking the thyroid. Marina's TPO antibodies are greater than 400, far above the upper limit of 13.8, confirming that her hypothyroidism is autoimmune in nature, consistent with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. This is not a new finding given her existing diagnosis, but the very high level confirms ongoing active immune attack against the thyroid, which is why her medication dose may need periodic adjustment as thyroid function gradually declines.
biomarkers.low_causes: Absence of autoimmune thyroid disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, postpartum thyroiditis

biomarkers.name: Thyroglobulin Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies target thyroglobulin, the protein precursor to thyroid hormones. Marina's result of 5.1 is above the upper limit of 4.4, confirming the autoimmune thyroid picture alongside her strongly positive TPO antibodies. More than 80% of the population have undetectable levels of this antibody, so its presence further supports the Hashimoto's diagnosis.
biomarkers.low_causes: Absence of autoimmune thyroid disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, thyroid cancer monitoring interference

biomarkers.name: Cortisol
biomarkers.description: Cortisol is the body's primary stress hormone, produced by the adrenal glands. It follows a circadian rhythm, peaking in the morning to help wake the body and declining through the day. Marina's cortisol of 297 is within the optimal morning range, suggesting her adrenal function and stress response are normal.
biomarkers.low_causes: Adrenal insufficiency, Addison's disease, pituitary disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic stress, Cushing's syndrome, corticosteroid use, acute illness

biomarkers.name: Oestradiol
biomarkers.description: Oestradiol is the primary oestrogen hormone, essential for reproductive function, bone density, cardiovascular protection, and brain health. Marina's oestradiol of 228 is within the follicular phase range of 71.6 to 529.2, suggesting she is in the follicular phase of her menstrual cycle. This is a healthy level and shows no sign of premature ovarian decline.
biomarkers.low_causes: Menopause, premature ovarian failure, extreme exercise or low body weight, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Ovarian cysts, oestrogen-producing tumours, obesity, hormone replacement therapy

biomarkers.name: Progesterone
biomarkers.description: Progesterone is the hormone produced primarily after ovulation by the corpus luteum. It supports the second half of the menstrual cycle and is essential for pregnancy. Marina's progesterone of 2.16 is within the follicular phase range of 0 to 4.45, which is expected given that progesterone is naturally low during the first half of the cycle before ovulation.
biomarkers.low_causes: Follicular phase of cycle (normal), anovulation, premature ovarian failure
biomarkers.high_causes: Luteal phase, pregnancy, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, ovarian cysts

biomarkers.name: Luteinising Hormone
biomarkers.description: Luteinising hormone (LH) is produced by the pituitary gland and triggers ovulation in women. Marina's LH of 8.72 is within the follicular phase range, consistent with normal reproductive function. An LH level in the follicular range at age 40 is reassuring and does not suggest perimenopause.
biomarkers.low_causes: Pituitary disease, stress, eating disorders, hypothalamic amenorrhoea
biomarkers.high_causes: Menopause, perimenopause, PCOS, pituitary tumour

biomarkers.name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone
biomarkers.description: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) drives the development of egg-containing follicles in the ovaries. Marina's FSH of 13.09 is above the follicular phase upper limit of 10.2 but well below the postmenopausal threshold of 23. A mildly elevated FSH at age 40 may reflect early ovarian reserve changes, which are a normal part of reproductive ageing. It could also represent a mid-cycle surge if her sample was taken near ovulation. This does not indicate menopause or perimenopause on its own, particularly as her LH is within range and her oestradiol is healthy.
biomarkers.low_causes: Pituitary disease, stress, eating disorders, hypothalamic amenorrhoea
biomarkers.high_causes: Perimenopause, menopause, premature ovarian failure, midcycle surge

biomarkers.name: Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone in women is produced by the ovaries and adrenal glands. While present in much smaller amounts than in men, it is important for muscle maintenance, bone density, libido, energy, and mood. Marina's testosterone of 0.9 is within the laboratory range but below the optimal floor of 1.0. Given her goal of building muscle and her low energy, optimising testosterone into the upper half of the range would be supportive. Physical activity, particularly resistance training, is one of the most effective ways to naturally support testosterone levels in women.
biomarkers.low_causes: Ageing, hypothyroidism, low physical activity, adrenal insufficiency, oral contraceptives
biomarkers.high_causes: PCOS, adrenal hyperplasia, ovarian or adrenal tumours, exogenous testosterone

biomarkers.name: Free Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Free testosterone is the fraction not bound to proteins (SHBG or albumin) and is the biologically active portion available to enter cells. Marina's free testosterone of 0.013 is within the laboratory range but below the optimal floor of 0.015. This is consistent with her total testosterone being below optimal and reflects low overall androgenic activity.
biomarkers.low_causes: High SHBG, low total testosterone, ageing, hypothyroidism
biomarkers.high_causes: PCOS, low SHBG, exogenous testosterone

biomarkers.name: Free Androgen Index
biomarkers.description: The Free Androgen Index (FAI) is a ratio of total testosterone to SHBG, providing another estimate of biologically available testosterone. Marina's FAI of 1.98 is within the laboratory range. For a woman, a mid-range FAI is normal and does not suggest androgen excess.
biomarkers.low_causes: High SHBG, low testosterone, oral contraceptives
biomarkers.high_causes: PCOS, low SHBG, exogenous androgens

biomarkers.name: SHBG
biomarkers.description: Sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) is a protein produced by the liver that binds to sex hormones, including testosterone and oestradiol, regulating how much is freely available to tissues. Marina's SHBG of 45.5 is within the optimal range. This is a healthy level that is neither excessively binding her testosterone nor leaving too much free.
biomarkers.low_causes: Obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism, PCOS
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism, liver disease, oestrogen use, ageing, low BMI

biomarkers.name: DHEA Sulphate
biomarkers.description: DHEA-S (dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate) is the most abundant steroid hormone in the body, produced primarily by the adrenal glands. It serves as a precursor to both testosterone and oestrogen. Marina's DHEA-S of 4.7 umol/L (approximately 1,732 ug/dL) is within the optimal range, indicating healthy adrenal function. DHEA-S naturally declines with age, so a solid mid-range level at 40 is a positive finding.
biomarkers.low_causes: Ageing, adrenal insufficiency, chronic illness
biomarkers.high_causes: Adrenal hyperplasia, PCOS, adrenal tumour

biomarkers.name: Prolactin
biomarkers.description: Prolactin is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland, primarily known for its role in milk production but also involved in immune regulation and reproductive function. Marina's prolactin of 130 is within the optimal non-pregnant range, ruling out prolactinoma (a benign pituitary tumour) and confirming normal pituitary function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Dopamine agonist medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Pituitary tumour, medications (antipsychotics, antidepressants), hypothyroidism, stress

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D 25(OH)
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption, bone health, immune function, muscle strength, and mood regulation. It is produced in the skin in response to sunlight and is difficult to obtain in sufficient quantities from diet alone. Marina's vitamin D of 71 is sufficient (above 50) but below the optimal threshold of 75 nmol/L. Given her symptoms of fatigue and hair thinning, and her goal of building muscle, bringing this into the optimal range of 75 to 120 would be beneficial. At her low BMI, 2,000 IU daily should be sufficient.
biomarkers.low_causes: Insufficient sunlight exposure, inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption, dark skin, obesity
biomarkers.high_causes: Excess supplementation, granulomatous disease

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone
biomarkers.description: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is produced by the four small parathyroid glands behind the thyroid. It regulates calcium levels in the blood by increasing calcium absorption from the gut, releasing calcium from bones, and reducing calcium excretion by the kidneys. Marina's PTH of 2.831 is within the optimal range, confirming that her calcium regulation is working properly and that her vitamin D level, while suboptimal, is not low enough to trigger a compensatory PTH rise.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypoparathyroidism, excess calcium, excess vitamin D, magnesium deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, calcium deficiency

biomarkers.name: Vitamin B12
biomarkers.description: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation, nerve function, DNA synthesis, and energy metabolism. Marina's B12 of 427 is within the laboratory range but below the optimal floor of 500. Given her existing iron deficiency and its impact on red blood cell production, ensuring B12 is optimal would support recovery once iron is replaced. Sublingual methylcobalamin at 1,000mcg daily is the recommended form.
biomarkers.low_causes: Dietary insufficiency (especially vegan/vegetarian), pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, metformin use
biomarkers.high_causes: Supplementation, liver disease, myeloproliferative disorders

biomarkers.name: Serum Folate (Vitamin B9)
biomarkers.description: Folate (vitamin B9) is essential for DNA synthesis, cell division, and red blood cell formation. It works closely with B12. Marina's folate of 18 is marginally above the upper limit of 17, which simply reflects good dietary intake or supplementation and is not a concern. High folate alongside adequate B12 supports healthy red blood cell production, which will be important as her iron stores are replenished.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary intake, alcohol, malabsorption, pregnancy, certain medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Supplementation, high vegetable intake, B12 deficiency masking (rare)

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase
biomarkers.description: Creatine kinase (CK) is an enzyme found in muscles (skeletal and cardiac) and the brain. It leaks into the blood when muscle tissue is damaged. Marina's CK of 64 is within the optimal range, confirming no significant muscle damage or inflammation. Given that she is not currently exercising, this low level is expected.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low muscle mass, sedentary lifestyle
biomarkers.high_causes: Intense exercise, muscle injury, myositis, statin use, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: IgG
biomarkers.description: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin in the blood, providing long-term immunity against previously encountered infections. Marina's IgG of 15.7 is within the laboratory range but near the upper limit of 16. In the context of her active autoimmune thyroid disease, a mildly elevated IgG is expected and reflects chronic immune activation rather than a separate immunological problem.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency, medications, protein-losing conditions
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, liver disease, myeloma

biomarkers.name: IgM
biomarkers.description: IgM is the first antibody produced in response to a new infection or immune challenge. It is the largest antibody and is particularly effective at activating the complement system. Marina's IgM of 3.5 is above the upper limit of 3.0. A modest IgM elevation can be seen in autoimmune disease, recent or recurrent infection, or as a normal individual variant. In Marina's case, the most likely explanation is her ongoing autoimmune thyroid disease. If this remains persistently elevated on future testing, her GP may wish to exclude other causes.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Acute or chronic infection, autoimmune disease, primary biliary cholangitis, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia

biomarkers.name: IgA
biomarkers.description: IgA is the immunoglobulin that protects mucosal surfaces including the gut, lungs, and urinary tract. Marina's IgA of 1.9 is comfortably within the normal range, confirming adequate mucosal immunity. Importantly, her IgA being within range means that her coeliac screen (tissue transglutaminase IgA) is reliable, as IgA deficiency can cause false negative coeliac results.
biomarkers.low_causes: Selective IgA deficiency (genetic), immunodeficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, liver disease, coeliac disease, IgA nephropathy

biomarkers.name: IgE
biomarkers.description: IgE is the immunoglobulin associated with allergic responses and parasitic infections. Marina's IgE of 12 is well within range and low, indicating no significant allergic sensitisation or parasitic burden.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding, immunodeficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergies, asthma, eczema, parasitic infection, drug reactions

biomarkers.name: Rheumatoid Factor
biomarkers.description: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an autoantibody that can be elevated in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune conditions. Marina's RF of 6 is within the normal range of below 14, providing reassurance that there is no serological evidence of rheumatoid arthritis.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, chronic infection, other autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: Tissue Transglutaminase IgA
biomarkers.description: Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) is the primary screening test for coeliac disease, an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten that damages the lining of the small intestine. Marina's result of 0.38 is well within the negative range, and her IgA level is normal, so the test is reliable. This effectively rules out coeliac disease as a cause of her fatigue, hair thinning, or any malabsorption (though iron absorption could be affected by other factors).
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding (no coeliac disease)
biomarkers.high_causes: Coeliac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis

biomarkers.name: Total Antioxidant Activity
biomarkers.description: Total antioxidant activity measures the overall capacity of the blood to neutralise free radicals, the unstable molecules that damage cells and accelerate ageing. Marina's TAA of 1.51 is within the optimal range, indicating adequate antioxidant protection.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor diet, oxidative stress, chronic disease, smoking
biomarkers.high_causes: Antioxidant supplementation, high fruit and vegetable intake, uric acid elevation

biomarkers.name: CA-125
biomarkers.description: CA-125 is a protein that can be elevated in ovarian cancer but is also raised by many benign conditions including endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, and even during menstruation. Marina's CA-125 of 31.4 is within the normal range of below 35. It is at the upper end of range, which can be influenced by the menstrual cycle phase. In a 40-year-old premenopausal woman, this level is not concerning.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Ovarian cancer, endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, menstruation, pregnancy

biomarkers.name: CA 15-3
biomarkers.description: CA 15-3 is a tumour marker primarily used in monitoring breast cancer. It is not a screening test and can be elevated by benign conditions. Marina's CA 15-3 of 11.13 is well within the normal range, which is reassuring.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Breast cancer, ovarian cancer, liver disease, benign breast conditions

biomarkers.name: CA 19-9
biomarkers.description: CA 19-9 is a tumour marker most commonly associated with pancreatic and biliary cancers. It can also be elevated by benign conditions such as gallstones, pancreatitis, and liver disease. Marina's CA 19-9 of 22.22 is within the normal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Pancreatic cancer, biliary cancer, pancreatitis, gallstones, liver disease

biomarkers.name: CEA
biomarkers.description: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a protein that can be elevated in colorectal and other cancers, as well as in smokers and some benign conditions. Marina's CEA of below 0.5 is very low and well within the normal non-smoker range, which is reassuring.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Colorectal cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, smoking, inflammatory bowel disease

biomarkers.name: Urine pH
biomarkers.description: Urine pH reflects the acidity or alkalinity of the urine. A pH of 6 is mildly acidic, which is within the normal physiological range of 4.5 to 8.0. This is a normal finding.
biomarkers.low_causes: High protein diet, metabolic acidosis, dehydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Vegetarian diet, urinary tract infection, renal tubular acidosis, alkalosis

biomarkers.name: Urine Protein
biomarkers.description: Protein in the urine (proteinuria) can indicate kidney damage. Marina's result is negative, confirming that her kidneys are not leaking protein and supporting the excellent kidney function seen in her blood markers.
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, urinary tract infection, dehydration, intense exercise, fever

biomarkers.name: Urine Ketones
biomarkers.description: Ketones appear in the urine when the body is burning fat for fuel instead of glucose, which can occur during fasting, very low carbohydrate diets, or uncontrolled diabetes. Marina's result is negative, indicating normal glucose metabolism.
biomarkers.high_causes: Fasting, ketogenic diet, diabetic ketoacidosis, prolonged vomiting

biomarkers.name: Urine Glucose
biomarkers.description: Glucose in the urine (glycosuria) occurs when blood sugar exceeds the kidney's reabsorption threshold, typically above 10 mmol/L. Marina's result is negative, consistent with her normal fasting glucose and HbA1c.
biomarkers.high_causes: Diabetes, renal glycosuria, pregnancy, corticosteroid use

biomarkers.name: Specific Gravity
biomarkers.description: Specific gravity measures the concentration of the urine, reflecting hydration status. Marina's specific gravity of 1.02 is within the normal range of 1.005 to 1.030, indicating adequate hydration.
biomarkers.low_causes: Overhydration, diabetes insipidus
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, SIADH, heart failure, kidney disease

biomarkers.name: Urobilinogen
biomarkers.description: Urobilinogen is a breakdown product of bilirubin. Small amounts in urine are normal. Marina's result is negative, which is a normal finding and confirms that her elevated bilirubin (consistent with Gilbert's syndrome) is not causing excess urobilinogen production.
biomarkers.low_causes: Bile duct obstruction, broad-spectrum antibiotic use
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemolytic anaemia, liver disease, hepatitis

biomarkers.name: Urine Casts
biomarkers.description: Urinary casts are cylindrical structures formed in the kidney tubules. Their presence can indicate various kidney conditions. Marina's result is negative, confirming healthy kidney tubular function.
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, dehydration, nephritis, nephrotic syndrome

biomarkers.name: Urine WBC
biomarkers.description: White blood cells in the urine can indicate a urinary tract infection or kidney inflammation. Marina's result of less than 1 is well below the significant threshold of 10, confirming no urinary tract infection or inflammation.
biomarkers.high_causes: Urinary tract infection, kidney infection, interstitial nephritis

biomarkers.name: Urine RBC
biomarkers.description: Red blood cells in the urine (haematuria) can indicate kidney stones, infection, or more serious urological conditions. Marina's result of less than 1 is well below the significant threshold of 25, confirming no blood in the urine.
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney stones, urinary tract infection, menstrual contamination, bladder or kidney cancer, glomerulonephritis

biomarkers.name: Urine Nitrites
biomarkers.description: Nitrites in the urine are produced by certain bacteria that convert dietary nitrates. A positive result suggests a bacterial urinary tract infection. Marina's result is negative, supporting the absence of infection.
biomarkers.high_causes: Bacterial urinary tract infection (gram-negative organisms)

biomarkers.name: Bacterial Count
biomarkers.description: The bacterial count measures the number of bacteria in the urine sample. This result is pending and will be reviewed when available. Given that Marina's urine WBCs, RBCs, and nitrites are all negative, a clinically significant infection is unlikely.
biomarkers.high_causes: Urinary tract infection, sample contamination

biomarkers.name: Urine Culture and Sensitivities
biomarkers.description: The urine culture identifies any bacteria present and determines which antibiotics they are sensitive to. This result is pending. Given the clean urinalysis findings (no WBCs, no nitrites, no blood), a positive culture is not expected.
biomarkers.high_causes: Urinary tract infection

biomarkers.name: Absolute Reticulocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells freshly released from the bone marrow, and their count reflects how actively the marrow is producing new red cells. A result of 36.9 against a lower limit of 50 means the marrow is producing fewer new red cells than it should. In Marina's case this is almost certainly driven by iron deficiency: the marrow has the machinery to make red cells but lacks the raw material. This suppressed output is one reason her haemoglobin is barely holding at its lower boundary.
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemolytic anaemia, blood loss with recovery, response to iron or B12 treatment
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12 or folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: Mentzer Index
biomarkers.description: Mentzer Index is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.low_causes: Thalassaemia trait
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency

biomarkers.name: Reticulocyte Production Index
biomarkers.description: Reticulocyte Production Index is reported for context only and is not applicable at present, so it is not flagged.
biomarkers.low_causes: Marrow not responding to anaemia: iron, B12 or folate deficiency, marrow suppression
biomarkers.high_causes: Blood loss or haemolysis with an appropriate marrow response

biomarkers.name: VLDL Cholesterol (Calculated)
biomarkers.description: VLDL, or very low-density lipoprotein, is the particle the liver packages triglycerides into for transport through the bloodstream. It is calculated from the triglyceride level. At 0.34, it sits well within range and reflects the healthy triglyceride result. VLDL itself contributes a small component to total cholesterol and to remnant cholesterol risk, but at this level it is not adding meaningful cardiovascular risk.
biomarkers.high_causes: Hypertriglyceridaemia, insulin resistance, excess carbohydrate intake, alcohol
biomarkers.low_causes: Very low fat intake, malnutrition

biomarkers.name: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL
biomarkers.description: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL is calculated from your measured results. It sits outside the ideal range. It is being driven by LDL Cholesterol, which sits outside the ideal range.
biomarkers.high_causes: Diet high in saturated fat, familial hypercholesterolaemia

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
biomarkers.description: Atherogenic Index of Plasma is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.high_causes: High triglycerides, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II)
biomarkers.description: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II) is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.high_causes: Raised LDL, low HDL

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
biomarkers.description: Total iron binding capacity measures the maximum amount of iron that the blood's transport proteins, primarily transferrin, could carry if fully loaded. When iron stores fall, the body upregulates transferrin production in an effort to capture more iron from the gut and tissues, driving TIBC upward. At 77.4 against an upper limit of 76.1, Marina's TIBC is elevated, which is exactly the pattern expected in iron deficiency and confirms the body is actively searching for more iron than it can find. This result reinforces the severity of the deficiency already described.
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, oral contraceptive use
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron overload, haemochromatosis, anaemia of chronic disease, malnutrition, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Fasting Insulin
biomarkers.description: Fasting insulin reflects how much insulin the pancreas is secreting when the body has not recently eaten. Insulin is the hormone that moves glucose from the bloodstream into cells for energy or storage. At 7.74, Marina's insulin sits within both the laboratory range and the optimal band of 2 to 8, indicating the pancreas is not overproducing insulin in the fasted state. In the context of her mildly elevated HOMA-IR, this suggests the issue is subtle rather than a frank excess of insulin secretion.
biomarkers.high_causes: Insulin resistance, early type 2 diabetes, obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, excess refined carbohydrate intake
biomarkers.low_causes: Low carbohydrate diet, type 1 diabetes, pancreatic insufficiency, prolonged fasting

biomarkers.name: Estimated Average Glucose
biomarkers.description: Estimated Average Glucose is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.high_causes: Prediabetes, type 2 diabetes

biomarkers.name: TyG Index
biomarkers.description: TyG Index is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.high_causes: Insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
biomarkers.description: Parathyroid hormone is produced by four small glands behind the thyroid and acts as the body's calcium regulator. When blood calcium falls, PTH rises to mobilise calcium from bone and increase its absorption from the gut. At 2.831, Marina's PTH sits comfortably within range and within the optimal band, indicating her calcium regulation is working appropriately and there is no evidence of parathyroid overactivity or underactivity.
biomarkers.high_causes: Primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, calcium malabsorption
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypoparathyroidism, hypercalcaemia from non-parathyroid causes, excess vitamin D supplementation

biomarkers.name: Free T4 (Thyroxine)
biomarkers.description: Free T4 is the circulating form of thyroxine, the main hormone produced by the thyroid gland and replaced by levothyroxine in those with hypothyroidism. At 19.9, it sits right at the top of the optimal range of 14 to 20 and well within the laboratory range, indicating that Marina's levothyroxine is delivering adequate T4 into the bloodstream. The fact that TSH remains elevated despite this adequate T4 level suggests the pituitary is still detecting suboptimal thyroid economy overall, possibly because conversion to the active T3 form is not fully efficient.
biomarkers.high_causes: Levothyroxine over-replacement, hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypothyroidism, inadequate levothyroxine dose, pituitary dysfunction

biomarkers.name: TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone)
biomarkers.description: TSH is the signal the pituitary gland sends to the thyroid to tell it to produce more hormone. When thyroid output is insufficient, TSH rises. At 6.41 against an upper limit of 4.78, Marina's TSH is above range despite her being on levothyroxine, indicating that her current dose is not fully suppressing pituitary stimulation. This is important because even mildly elevated TSH is associated with fatigue, hair thinning, difficulty building muscle, and impaired LDL clearance, all of which are directly relevant to her symptoms and goals.
biomarkers.high_causes: Hypothyroidism, inadequate levothyroxine dose, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, pituitary TSH-secreting tumour (rare)
biomarkers.low_causes: Hyperthyroidism, levothyroxine over-replacement, pituitary dysfunction

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies (TPO)
biomarkers.description: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are produced when the immune system mistakenly targets an enzyme essential for thyroid hormone production. A result of greater than 400 against an upper limit of 13.8 is markedly elevated and confirms significant autoimmune activity directed at the thyroid gland. This level of antibody titre is strongly consistent with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the autoimmune condition that is the most common cause of hypothyroidism. The ongoing immune attack gradually reduces the thyroid's own hormone-producing capacity over time, which is why levothyroxine doses often require upward adjustment as the condition progresses.
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, other autoimmune conditions
biomarkers.low_causes: Not clinically significant

biomarkers.name: Thyroglobulin Antibody
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies target thyroglobulin, the protein scaffolding the thyroid uses to assemble thyroid hormone. At 5.1 against an upper limit of 4.4, this result is modestly above range. In isolation the elevation is mild, but in combination with the strongly positive TPO antibodies it further supports the autoimmune thyroid pattern. Together, the two positive antibody results point consistently toward Hashimoto's thyroiditis as the underlying cause of Marina's hypothyroidism.
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, differentiated thyroid cancer (in the context of monitoring after treatment)
biomarkers.low_causes: Not clinically significant

biomarkers.name: FT3:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: FT3:FT4 Ratio is calculated from your measured results. It sits outside the ideal range. It is being driven by TSH, which sits outside the ideal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor T4 to T3 conversion, low ferritin or selenium, chronic illness
biomarkers.high_causes: Overactive thyroid, stimulant use

biomarkers.name: CEA (Carcinoembryonic Antigen)
biomarkers.description: CEA is a protein that can be produced by certain cancer cells, particularly those of the colon, rectum, lung, and breast. It is used primarily to monitor known cancers rather than as a screening tool, as many benign conditions can also raise it. A result of less than 0.5 against an upper limit of 5 is reassuringly low and rules out any meaningful elevation.
biomarkers.high_causes: Colorectal, lung, breast or pancreatic cancer, heavy smoking, inflammatory bowel disease, liver disease
biomarkers.low_causes: Not clinically significant

biomarkers.name: SHBG (Sex Hormone Binding Globulin)
biomarkers.description: Sex hormone binding globulin is a protein produced by the liver that binds to testosterone and oestrogen in the bloodstream, making them temporarily unavailable for use by tissues. At 45.5, Marina's SHBG sits comfortably within both the laboratory range and the optimal band, meaning neither too much nor too little of her sex hormones are being bound and rendered inactive. SHBG tends to rise with thyroid hormone excess and fall with insulin resistance or obesity, so its position within range here is consistent with the overall hormonal picture.
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism, liver disease, oestrogen excess, low BMI, ageing
biomarkers.low_causes: Insulin resistance, obesity, hypothyroidism, excess androgen

biomarkers.name: Free Testosterone (Calculated)
biomarkers.description: Free testosterone is the small fraction of total testosterone not bound to SHBG or albumin and therefore directly available to tissues. It is calculated from total testosterone and SHBG rather than measured directly. At 0.013 nmol/L, the result falls within the laboratory range but at the lower portion of it and below the optimal floor of 0.02. Low free testosterone in women is associated with reduced libido, low energy, and difficulty building muscle. Given Marina's goals of building muscle and improving energy, it is worth monitoring, though the most actionable priority remains the iron and thyroid corrections first.
biomarkers.high_causes: Polycystic ovary syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumour, anabolic steroid use
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, elevated SHBG, hypopituitarism, menopause

biomarkers.name: Bioavailable Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Bioavailable Testosterone is calculated from your measured results. It is within the ideal range, as are the results it is calculated from.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, poor sleep, chronic stress
biomarkers.high_causes: Testosterone therapy, anabolic steroid use

biomarkers.name: Urine WBCs
biomarkers.description: White blood cells in the urine indicate immune activity in the urinary tract, which is the hallmark finding in a genuine urinary tract infection. A count of fewer than 1 per microlitre means there are effectively no white cells present, which argues strongly against active infection or inflammation in the urinary tract.

biomarkers.name: Urine RBCs
biomarkers.description: Red blood cells in the urine, known as haematuria, can indicate bleeding anywhere along the urinary tract. A count of fewer than 1 per microlitre means there is effectively no blood in the urine sample, which is a reassuring finding and does not require further investigation.

biomarkers.name: Mecillinam Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Mecillinam is an antibiotic used specifically for urinary tract infections caused by certain gram-negative bacteria including E. coli. A sensitive result means that if treatment were required, the organism identified in the culture would be effectively killed by this antibiotic. This forms part of the antibiogram returned alongside the urine culture.

biomarkers.name: Temocillin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Temocillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic with activity against resistant gram-negative organisms. An intermediate result means the organism has reduced susceptibility and temocillin would not be the first choice for treatment. This is noted for completeness as part of the antibiogram.

biomarkers.name: Ampicillin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Ampicillin resistance is very common among urinary E. coli isolates and does not indicate a particularly aggressive or unusual organism. It means ampicillin would not be an effective treatment choice should antibiotic therapy be required.

biomarkers.name: Amoxicillin/Clavulanic Acid Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Resistance to amoxicillin combined with clavulanic acid (co-amoxiclav or Augmentin) is also common in urinary isolates and narrows the oral antibiotic options if treatment were needed. This is noted for the GP's reference alongside the other antibiogram results.

biomarkers.name: Piperacillin/Tazobactam Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Piperacillin combined with tazobactam is a broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic used for more complex infections. A sensitive result means the organism would respond to this agent if intravenous treatment were ever required. It is not relevant to outpatient management.

biomarkers.name: Cefixime Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Cefixime is an oral third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that can be used to treat urinary tract infections. A sensitive result means the identified organism would respond to this agent, providing an oral treatment option alongside mecillinam and nitrofurantoin.

biomarkers.name: Ceftazidime Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Ceftazidime is an intravenous cephalosporin used for more serious infections. A sensitive result is noted for completeness as part of the full antibiogram returned by the laboratory.

biomarkers.name: Ceftriaxone Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Ceftriaxone is an intravenous cephalosporin commonly used when oral therapy is not appropriate. Sensitivity to this agent is noted as part of the antibiogram for the GP's reference.

biomarkers.name: Ertapenem Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Ertapenem is a carbapenem antibiotic reserved for resistant gram-negative infections. Sensitivity here indicates the organism has not developed carbapenem resistance, which is reassuring from an antimicrobial stewardship perspective.

biomarkers.name: Meropenem Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Meropenem is another carbapenem antibiotic used for serious hospital-acquired infections. Sensitivity is noted as part of the complete antibiogram. It is not relevant to outpatient management of a urinary isolate in Marina's clinical context.

biomarkers.name: Amikacin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used intravenously for resistant gram-negative infections. Sensitivity to amikacin is part of the full antibiogram and is noted for completeness.

biomarkers.name: Gentamicin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside used intravenously for serious urinary and systemic infections. A sensitive result is noted for the GP's reference as part of the antibiogram.

biomarkers.name: Ciprofloxacin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with good urinary penetration and oral bioavailability, commonly used for urinary tract infections. Sensitivity means it would be an effective treatment option, though fluoroquinolones are generally reserved for cases where first-line agents are not suitable.

biomarkers.name: Fosfomycin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Fosfomycin is an oral antibiotic used as a single-dose treatment for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections. Sensitivity means it would be an effective first-line oral option alongside mecillinam and nitrofurantoin, and its convenient single-dose regimen makes it a practical choice if treatment is needed.

biomarkers.name: Nitrofurantoin Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Nitrofurantoin is a first-line oral antibiotic for uncomplicated urinary tract infections, with activity concentrated in the urinary tract. Sensitivity confirms it would be an effective treatment option. Along with mecillinam and fosfomycin, this gives Marina's GP a clear choice of appropriate oral agents if treatment becomes indicated.

biomarkers.name: Trimethoprim Sensitivity
biomarkers.description: Trimethoprim resistance is increasingly common among urinary E. coli isolates in the UK and Ireland. This means trimethoprim should not be used for treatment if antibiotic therapy is required. The GP should select from the sensitive agents instead.
